utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday, the 25th of June, 2007. I'd like to greet everyone in this courtroom. I'd like to greet the Prosecution and especially Mr. Mundis. I'm very pleased to see him back with us after a very long period of absence. I would also like to greet the Defence counsel and the accused and, more particularly, Mr. Coric, who is back with us as well. I won't forget to mention all those helping us, assisting us here. I would like first to give the floor to the registrar for some IC or e-court numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, again, Your Honour. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Azra Krajsek. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 608; the list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 609; the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number 610; while the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number 611. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. I want us to move into private session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have three matters to raise. Well, I had three. I think I now have a fourth to raise. I will do so as briefly as possible. The first an oral application for an extension of time. There are, as you know, a number of motions filed by the Prosecution relating to the admission of documents and witness statements which the Defence is trying to deal with on a joint basis. We hope to submit joint responses for each of these because we know that's the Trial Chamber's preference and ours as well. And all of these motions involve a great deal of documentary reading, of course, and analysis. I'm responsible for compiling a response on the motion for admission of certain statements under Rule 92 bis pertaining to the municipalities of Capljina and Stolac, and, Your Honour, my application would be that the deadline for those -- for that motion, to respond to that motion, be the same as Your Honours have already granted in two other cases and that it be deferred until the 12th of July. So I would make that oral application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We grant the application made by the Defence, and you will have until the 12th of July 4.25 to file your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. Your Honour, the second matter is one I hadn't intended to mention but really has arisen today when Your Honours made the decision regarding the present witness to reduce the amount of time available to the Defence from eight hours to six hours. Your Honour, I make this observation: When the Trial Chamber does this at the last moment, it not only hinders the Defence in preparing efficiently for cross-examination of the witness, but it also deprives us of necessary time. The -- it also places our fate in the Prosecution's hands, because it means whenever the Prosecution decides belatedly to reduce the time devoted to direct examination, they know at the same time they can reduce the time for cross-examination. Your Honour, with this particular witness, and I think in the case of most witnesses, the -- the time necessary for a proper direct and for a proper cross are not logically related. It really does not hinder the Prosecution's presentation of its case very much, if at all, to reduce the amount of time for a direct examination. In fact, in many cases they can and have taken a witness originally scheduled as a viva voce witness and dealt with the witness under 92 ter with a certain amount of viva voce direct examination. And if it means, Your Honour, that at the Prosecution's discretion they can come in on a particular day and say, by the way, we've decided to reduce the time by two or three hours and we expect the Trial Chamber now to reduce the time for cross-examination by the Defence, it places the right of the accused to cross-examine within the Prosecution's control and, Your Honour, that, with all due respect, is not a fair way to run the trial and it prejudices the Defence because we're now in a position of having less time than we need and thought we would have. And I would ask Your Honours to take the position that if the Prosecution decides to reduce the time, nonetheless the Defence should have the time originally allocated for cross-examination. The time is available. We are going to be sitting this week. The witness is scheduled for this week, and it can do no harm whatsoever either to the trial schedule or to the Prosecution to give the Defence full time for cross-examination. So I ask the Trial Chamber to please reflect upon that and perhaps to reconsider that -- that decision. Your Honour, the remaining two matters are matters that arose during the hearing on the 20th of June and on which we seek the Trial Chamber's guidance. The Trial Chamber will remember firstly that during cross-examination of last week's witness, His Honour Judge Trechsel indicated that the Trial Chamber's view of its ruling of the 13th of November was that the tendering of documents through examination of a witness operated rather differently in the case of the Prosecution than the way it does in the case of the Defence and that ordinarily it might not be possible for the Defence to tender documents through cross-examination of a witness, certainly in a case where the witness did not -- well, there might be a misunderstanding. Your Honour, let me just put this it this day: I think there is an uncertainty among the ranks of the Defence as to where that issue stands and we would appreciate just a clarification. I don't mean immediately but within a short time, perhaps as to the true meaning of that order so that we -- we know where we stand in regard to the use of documents on cross-examination. That can be done, I think, by way of oral clarification. We would appreciate that because otherwise it's difficult for us to know how to conduct the cross-examination. The last matter, Your Honour, is -- is this: It's -- I want to put this matter as delicately as I can. It is a somewhat delicate matter. During the same hearing an issue arose regarding the treatment of the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia, and some discussion developed during cross-examination about the treatment of refugees generally, including at other place where is they might have been held, and I -- I recall that during that discussion there was an intervention by His Honour Judge Prandler. This is at page 78, line 25 through page 79, line 21, in which His Honour seemed to suggest that he had personally been present during -- at a camp or more than one camp in Hungary where such refugees were being held and was in a position to comment on the conditions under which they were being held there. And, Your Honour, our concern is only this, really, that clearly inevitably from time to time there will be a situation where a Judge from the Tribunal has some personal knowledge of facts that might be relevant to the Trial Chamber's decision. Obviously all the members of the Trial Chamber and of the Tribunal as a whole, the Judges, are men and women with long and distinguished careers in public life which have taken them into various duties in international law and diplomacy. But it becomes a matter of concern if there are facts within the knowledge of the Judge if the parties are unaware and which could, of course, ultimately bear on the factual findings that that Judge may be disposed to make. Obviously we don't know the extent of that; it may not be significant. But I would like to very respectfully invite Judge Prandler at a convenient moment to advise the parties as to the extent of any personal knowledge that he may have arising from his distinguished career on behalf of the Hungarian government or otherwise, just so we know where we stand on that and so there can be no question of the Judge perhaps substituting personal knowledge for the evidence. I hope, Your Honour, that I've put that respectfully. I intend it respectfully but it is matter which we would invite the Trial Chamber to consider. Your Honours, those are the matters I wanted to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to Judge Prandler, but with respect to points four of your comments, when Judge Prandler took the floor, as far as I understand he did so to stress that in a refugee camp you have a number of rules that apply. What he wanted to say, but of course he will give you further explanation about this, what he wanted to say is that a refugee camp works according to specific procedure, and his comment was made following another comment. I was not particularly surprised by this comment or this question. I myself had taken the floor previously and said that I was surprised to see that we had not been given all the laws, all the texts pertaining to the refugee status in Croatia, whereas we were dealing with the status of refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina with a witness who was only competent as far as refugees in Croatia. So that's the background in which you have to place the comments made by Judge Prandler, but of course he will answer himself. Now, as for your third point, what Judge Trechsel said about documents he will most probably respond himself, but as for the rules that apply in this, when the Defence cross-examine a witness they may submit a document to that particular witness and the document may be admitted. We've been doing so for about a year now. There is no ambiguity whatsoever as long as the document is relevant and reliable, the document may be admitted into evidence. I don't see any problem there. As for your second point, the reduction from eight to six hours. As I said last week, based on the information provided by the Prosecution, who thought that they needed six hours, we had decided that we would grant two extra hours to the Defence, but since the Prosecution has withdrawn 11 documents and reduced its time from six to four hours, we decided, so as not to prejudice the Prosecution, we decided to cut the time allocated to the Defence by two hours. Obviously if it appears necessary, if need be, and we'll see what happens during cross-examination, we might reconsider our position, but it will all depend on the relevance of this witness and what he says during examination-in-chief and cross-examination. And you also have to take into account the fact that a number of documents submitted or -- that will be submitted by the witness have already been -- by the Prosecution will have already been submitted to previous witnesses. Let me give the floor to Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the question which was asked and put by Mr. Murphy is, of course, an important one. As far as I know, a Judge is not obliged to clarify his or her position concerning some questions or comments, but nevertheless I would like to make a few observations on that issue. First of all, I would like to thank Maitre Murphy for his very polite way to raise this question, as he has already raised it during the -- that time when we talked about this issue last week. Let me first of all emphasise that I indeed had some knowledge and experience about the camps both as being involved with issues of -- of the former Yugoslav crisis, and also since I was also involved and in a way active in the field of the Hungarian Red Cross movement and the international aspects too. I mean, also at that time I had contacts with ICRC. On the other hand, I believe that the context that my question --, not my question, but my remark has been done is the following: That the Defence asked the lady, the witness, if in her view wasn't it the -- the treatment of the refugees the best in comparison with other countries. At least it is what I understood the question. I do not have before me now the record. But since this question was formulated in this way, if she, the witness, was aware of the very fact that in Croatia the treatment and approach to refugees was the best one from among those other countries where -- where refugees were accommodated, therefore I said in my view it is very difficult to ask a witness to determine the answer to this question since we have to speak and we have to speak about several countries, and as you know very well, those several countries included Slovenia, Austria, Hungary, Turkey, because Turkey was in a way counted -- in a way counted also among those countries and even probably, I'm not quite sure, but Bulgaria and some other countries also they were involved. So in this very complex situation, where there were hundreds of thousands of refugees abroad, when there were several countries, almost let's say, ten where refugees -- ten countries where refugees were given shelter, in my view it would have been really rather impossible for a witness who -- that with the refugees in Croatia, though, but she was not, as far as I know, she was not given the possibility to go to other countries and to check what is happening with the refugees in other countries. I really felt that this question was not very well considered, and therefore I said that -- that the very level of the treatment, in my view, is not to this expert -- I'm sorry, to this witness to determine because she -- she was mainly aware and dealt with the situation in Croatia. And I still maintain this, that -- that without any prejudice to the situation in Croatia I may admit the situation there was quite good. I do know, and I do recognise that the -- most of the refugees had been accommodated in Croatia. Nobody questions this, and it is not the issue. The issue was for me that in my view the witness cannot make a comparison between and among various countries which were in a way involved by giving shelter to the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Croatia proper, et cetera, et cetera. So it is my position, and therefore I do not think that I have to -- to go any further. I believe that my question was on the right wavelength with the situation which then prevailed, and I keep my position that this kind of comparison is very difficult to expect from someone who already worked in Croatia proper and not in other foreign countries. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, just dealing quickly with three matters, but starting with the point that Mr. Murphy made in relation to His Honour Judge Prandler. Your Honour, we -- we subscribe to the fairly simple essential point made by Mr. Murphy which is that where a Judge does have possession of knowledge outside just the normal commonsense scope of what the practical purpose is judicial notice that may relate to the case, then bearing in mind that the essential principle that cases must be decided on the evidence, then the request that in those circumstances that should be made clear to the parties, it's just a standing request and I say nothing at all about the particular detailed matter. We've heard Judge Prandler's explanation this afternoon. I certainly don't propose to criticise or pursue that particular matter but the general point we do subscribe to. Secondly, in relation to the point Mr. Murphy raised on the effect of the order in relation to documents. We're not entirely comfortable that the exchange yet covers that point so we would again support Mr. Murphy. It might be helpful if the Court were to look at the discussion last week, look at where we are on that, give us some indication as to where we stand and then if it is necessary to have some further submissions and discussion in court that we can deal with it. And then going back in effect of what might have been the first point on the list. The question of the time for examination-in-chief and cross-examination. Mr. President, you spoke in terms of avoiding prejudice to the Prosecution. Our submission is that that particular point is, with respect, fundamentally misconceived. Where the Prosecution are saying that they only need four hours for their evidence in chief, they have got what they want and need for the purposes of presenting their case so far as that witness is concerned, and the spurious equalities or near equalities and calculations by saying, well, it's either the same or it's some proportion or a proportionate reduction of the Defence time isn't achieving the essential purpose of allowing each party fairly to put its case. The Prosecution are saying they don't need more than four hours to present their evidence in chief. The Defence are saying we do still need, in this particular case, eight hours, and Your Honours, unless Your Honours are looking very specifically at the content to say, well, in the light where we now see matters have gone, it's clear the Defence don't actually need as much as they previously had. The position should stand as it has been directed in relation to time and Mr. Murphy's point is valid and it isn't any question of prejudice to the Prosecution. This idea that the Prosecution suffer prejudice if we get more time for cross-examination than had in chief is seriously flawed as an inflexible or even semi-flexible rule of thumb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel is going to answer as far as his concern and then we'll have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Murphy, I thank you for having raised this because quite apparently, it is a misunderstanding that has arisen. To the extent that I am responsible for that, which I do not exclude, I apologise. The issue that I referred to did not concern the presentation of documents during cross-examination at all. I only had in mind number 6 of our decision on the admissibility of evidence of 13 July 2006 which grants in the present phase of the proceedings to the Prosecution, but it is my assumption that when the Defence case is up it will be a similar rule for the Defence or an equal rule. But now it is only the Prosecution that by the virtue of this decision is given the possibility of introducing, under certain conditions and circumstances documents, they could not present to a witness outside a court hearing. I have recalled this, but there is no connection to cross-examination and to presenting documents during cross-examination. I hope this clarifies the matter, and I'm sure it's no surprise to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Judge Trechsel, and I appreciate the clarification. I just want to make sure that I understand it because I was, to be frank about this, I was under the -- maybe the misconception that where the Defence had documents that it believed it could use with a particular witness, but did not have sufficient time, the Defence would also have the opportunity to have those documents admitted under the same more or less criteria, that is, you have to state your reasons why you didn't present it to the witness, what the relevance is, and so on and so forth. That was my understanding. And I say that because there are times when we had a lot of documents that go to a particular witness that directly relate to the direct examination, not to a portion of the Defence case, for instance, and by that I mean something that one would be expected to put on if a Defence were to put on a case. And when we don't have sufficient time, I mean we're in this dilemma. You see, I understand the Judges' positions that the Defence lawyers, when conducting cross-examination, should not necessarily be putting on their case first, for instance, and then trying to rebut whatever evidence came in through direct examination, but, rather, they should be conducting the cross-examination on the basis of what the Prosecution has done. And that's why, for instance, the rule if you're going to go beyond the scope of direct examination, while you may do so, the circumstances should be such that you would -- you would ask open -- open-ended questions as opposed to leading questions. That's my understanding. So -- but I think if we have documents that directly relate to issues raised on cross-examination, but because of time limitations we are unable to confront the witness with these documents, the only other alternative we have is to bring that witness back during our case. So I just throw that out for your consideration. Maybe you have considered it, but in any event, to be honest that was my understanding. Maybe I didn't read guideline 6 correctly. That's number one. Number two, I just wanted to assure Judge Prandler that our concern, and of course we -- maybe we don't have to be concerned because we're dealing with professional Judges, but at least I was always trained that even the Judges, you know, because they're human, they shouldn't be bringing in experiences from outside and factoring that in as part of the evidence. Of course, in other words, if they have some medical knowledge and then there's medical testimony, expert testimony, they say, I discount this medical expert because my wife tells me who's a doctor, that such-and-such. In other words, the evidence comes from here. That's our concern. It's not an attack; it's just that, when we hear that sort of stuff, because of our training, a lightbulb goes off and we feel in the best interests of our clients, for transparency, we raise it. We mean no disrespect, we mean no harm. I think it was done in an appropriate manner and I hope Your Honour understands that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to stop this discussion because we have been discussing for close to three-quarters of an hour on procedural matters. We are going to look into what Mr. Karnavas rightly said. Guideline -- the guideline only dealt with Prosecution documents when they were presenting their case, and the decisions we made did not concern the Defence, but it may be that in certain cases there may be problems. Only last week or last time when Mr. Praljak told us that he had 95 binders on the issue that had been raised, that obviously he was not in a position to bring the 95 binders with hundreds of documents. Maybe in such a situation it might be wise to think of a procedure whereby, on the basis of the amount of documents, the Defence might be allowed to file in writing or to ask for these documents to be tendered when they are cross-examining a witness. We're going to look into this because this is a very complicated matter. We're going to discuss this in the hours to come. Yes, Ms. Alaburic. I see you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just two sentences from me with respect to the guidelines. I'd like to remind you that at a discussion of the 16th of November, 2006, the transcript pages were 9533 to 9542, we discussed this same topic then, and it was Mr. Murphy who raised it. I'm not going to quote his words, but he said that he considered that there was a mistake and that quite obviously in point 6 of the guidelines it should say "Parties" and not "Prosecution." And the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, said, and I'm going to quote, he said the following: "[In English] Third point, a technical one, and you are quite right there. We substitute the term 'Prosecution' for 'Parties'." So that, Your Honour, we considered that as of the 6th of November, 2006, this is an oral amendment to the guidelines, and that is why we were surprised to hear the interpretation by His Honour Judge Trechsel and what I just said and the quotation I made can be checked in the transcript of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to look into this matter very shortly, and we'll arrive at a solution, the most practical solution possible. We're going to have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you please state your first name, your surname, and your date of birth. Wits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first name is clause. I was born of the 10th of the 12th 1937. My family name is Nissen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a retired colonel from the German army in Germany, and I live mainly in Berlin. Otherwise, in Allgau in the south of Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you been a witness previously before an international tribunal as to the events at that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is this the first time that you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration handed over to you by Madam Usher. Please read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please sit down. Colonel, allow me to give you some explanations as to the way these hearing days are going to unfold for your testimony. First of all, you'll be answering questions put to you by the OTP representatives. I guess you met them yesterday or this morning. And you will be provided with documents to be found in binders. You'll find the numbers -- also the numbers of the documents, because each document has a number. Once the Prosecution has asked their questions, you have the Defence counsel on your left-hand side or the accused who can ask questions of you as part of the cross-examination. The three Judges who are in front of you can also ask questions of you as provided by the rules at any time, but we endeavour to put our questions once the parties have put theirs. But sometimes, exceptionally so, we do intervene because we have a document in front of us and we think it's necessary to ask our questions then. Please, try to be as precise as you can in your answers. If you fail to understand the meaning of a question, do not hesitate to ask the one asking that question to reformulate it. We have breaks every 90 minutes for 20 minutes so that you can have a rest. Also, to change the audiotapes. If at any time you do not feel well, do not hesitate to ask for a break. Also, I have learned that at times if questions deal with people that you met personally, that you know, then we can move into private session that their names do not appear or anything related to them appear in the transcript. I'm thinking of people you may have met as part of the mission you then carried out. So this is, generally speaking, the way the hearing is going to take place. I know also that you speak English perfectly, and French as well, which is good, because this will avoid any translation problems. You have a screen in front of you, and everything that is being said here is transcribed into English so that if need be you can look at it. But generally speaking, I had rather the witness looked at the person asking the question. I think it's much better that way. So the floor is yours, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everybody in courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. Colonel, if we may start with a few biographical details. You are retired from the German army. When did you retire therefrom?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I retired at the end of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How long had you -- had you served in the German army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Thirty-six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At the time when you retired what position were you occupying? In what section were you serving?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I was a colonel in the -- it's a department of the defence ministry in Bonn. I was head of department. And in the last 20 years, I was responsible for NBC defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what does NBC defence stand for?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. As I've just said, N for nuclear, B for biological, and C for chemical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. After your retirement, when did you become a monitor for the European Commission Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I became a monitor on the 1st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How did it come that you were appointed a monitor after your retirement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: It was presumably the German Foreign Ministry applied to the Ministry of Defence and asked that they would select a suitable person for this mission, and I was the person appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before going to the theatre of your mission did you is receive any briefings from the Foreign Ministry?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was an extremely short briefing, and it had to do with the procedures and formalities, not on the contents of the countries concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, now if we could just briefly look at the periods of your mission. When did you first arrive in -- in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, or when did you arrive in theatre for the first time round?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I started on the 1st of March, 1993, in Zagreb, and from there I was sent to Albania. I spent four weeks in Albania, in the north of Albania, in Fukespansuri [phoen] in the area near to Kosovo, and then approximately on the 1st of April, I came to Zagreb, to Split, and then to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and finally I was in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, there were flights, flight connections. We travelled with a car, with a shuttle. I think it was the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And during your period as a monitor, is it correct that you also took a period of leave?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I had a period of leave from about the 6th of May to the 25th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From your arrival on -- early in April until you departed on leave, were you in Siroki Brijeg or with a team associated with that area all the time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Our accommodation was in Siroki Brijeg, and there I was with a team, with another monitor, and with the then-head of the CC Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who was the then-head of the CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was Christopher Beese at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The other monitor on whom you were -- with whom you were on a team, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was Kiki Salamanca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, upon your return from leave where did you go then and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Then I went back to Siroki because this was our headquarters, and then there I started as the head of CC Mostar. I was responsible for this control centre, and this is where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Until when did you stay as the head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I was there until the end of this mission, and I completed this about the end of July, 25th, 26th of July, round about then, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who took over from you as the head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: The -- my follower was Sir Martin Garrod.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After this period when you left as head of CC Mostar did you then return to Germany?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I went back to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After returning to Germany did you ever return again for a further stint as a monitor?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I went on another mission to the same area, mainly to the same area from the 1st of June, 1994, until the 12th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can return to your period when you first arrived in Siroki Brijeg. What was the name of the team that you -- that you actually joined in CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, the CC Mostar at the time was called CC Grude because this is where it originated, but its headquarters were in Siroki Brijeg. And the team that I worked with, this was the M1 team, responsible more for the area of Jablanica and Konjic to the north of Mostar, but we were also partly active in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, the Court has already heard evidence about the structure of the CC Mostar team, so I will not go into that further with you. The Court has also heard of the reporting structure and the reporting system from the teams up to RC Zenica and further up to Zagreb and from there onwards, so I will also not deal with that aspect in detail. The one question I will ask you is during your period with this team, is it correct that there were regular reports that were written and which were sent up the chain of communication?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: There were daily reports. There were weekly summary reports, and in -- sometimes ad hoc reports if something had happened, and there were also sometimes reports which were a general overview of the region and the situation which were always reviewed and supplemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can look at the period when you arrived during April, I would like to focus first on the village of Doljani. Did you ever during April visit the village of Doljani or that area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I visited the area of Doljani several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How many times did you visit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, three times, I think at least. Certainly three times, maybe four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When was the first time you visited Doljani?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I must be rather careful with the dates. I can give you the approximate date from my memory, but I think it was round about the 7th or the 8th, yes, of April. Round about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: For what purpose did you visit Doljani at that time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was at a time -- first of all, it was for a general orientation of the overall area we were. Kiki Salamanca knew this in part; I knew it not at all. But the purpose was also to see for the first time to what extent rumours were true that the HVO were engaged in skirmishes from Jablanica towards Doljani, to see if this was true. This was the primary intention of going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what did you observe when you went there, if anything?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. We went into the village. We saw things going on as normally. We saw a few women on the streets, a few children were playing, chickens in the yards, and then on the bottom right there was a small river and near the river, there was a small path down, we saw some Croatian soldiers. We met them and we spoke to them. They were something like a company, a small firing post, and some of the names was Stipe Polje [as interpreted]. I just remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you say that you saw some Croatian soldiers, what do you mean by "Croatian soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I meant those soldiers who were at the firing post. I didn't see any in the village or in the houses or anywhere else, only at this post, just as calm as a firing post can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, but what I would like to know from you is you describe them as being Croatian soldiers, and I just want to check with you what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, I was imprecise, but I meant soldiers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when did you next return to Doljani?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was after the 15th of April. 17th, 18th of April, round about then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you describe to the Court what you observed at this time? And I would ask you not to describe any people by name. If that becomes necessary, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I saw -- first of all, there was an armija check-point. They had set up barricades at the entrance to the valley at a certain point. These were heavy barricades on the street, on the road, but you could still pass it with a small vehicle. When we arrived in Doljani, there wasn't an open fire but one house was burning, and the doors of the house were open. Part of another house were destroyed. This house seemed to have caved in. There were no civil people on the square. So this image of women and children as 10 days before. But there were HVO soldiers, and there was a leader, and they stopped us and the leader said, "You have nothing to do here. You should disappear." He didn't immediately threaten us, although he made us understand that this was his final statement and that we should not doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may briefly move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that you were prevented from going to Siroki -- I'm sorry, Sovici during that second visit. Did you at a later stage again try to go to Sovici?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: At a later moment I went to Sovici again -- no, I passed Sovici, to be precise. And it was at a time -- that was a few days later, quite a few days later. It was only possible with the Spanish Battalion, because the check-point that I've already mentioned was -- that had been closed with major blocks, barriers, and the Spanish Battalion used engineers and they pushed these blocks aside so that with a Spanish battle tank we could cross. And on that occasion we saw further houses that were destroyed in Doljani. Not that many, but some. And we took that road to the end of the valley without really seeing anything. Then we approached Sovici, and even then I didn't see any open firing there, but smoke and -- smoke in various places. We would have to go right into Sovici because Sovici is about two kilometres off the main road which leads then up to the mountains. And we were escorted by HVO soldiers, and they told us that in Sovici -- we shouldn't really go to Sovici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. There is a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, it seems that is technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's okay again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's okay again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: So we took that route which led up the mountain but couldn't go into Sovici where we saw fire or we saw smoke. We wouldn't go in there because we were escorted by HVO soldiers who told us to stay on this road that led up to the mountains, and the Spanish commander of the tank didn't really want to contravene what he had been told. Sovici is about two kilometres on the right-hand side. We then kept going up, up to the highest point where, from the valley of Doljani, there is the plain of Tomislav. And there was a big group of soldiers, HVO soldiers, in a mixture. They were a bit upset, a bit irritated, maybe because they had to stay behind, because we were coming along and soldiers, as they are, they were a bit impatient and teasing each other. Then the local leader told us we were not supposed to go to -- back to Doljani, but what we should do instead, we should go round to Tomislav, to what's Medjugorje, which would really be three times as far. This was just really to annoy us. We didn't do that. The commander of the battle tank agreed to turn round. So that was the end of this episode, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you recall how long after your second visit to Doljani this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kruger, I'm sorry. May I make an observation as to translation. You have spoken of a Schutzenpanzer. Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is a battle -- a battle tank but a lighter tank. It was a -- you could call it a personnel carrier. A kind of personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Exactly that. That is my point. It was translated by battle tank and I think that evokes a wrong impression. The better term would be APG, an Armoured Personnel Carrier. Would you agree with this? It's just for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, for that clarification, Your Honour, I think it's APC though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just to return to that last question, can you remember approximately how long after your second visit to Doljani this event took place?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I can't just try and limit the time. There was a further visit, but that I didn't take part in. That was on the 5th of May, after a longer conference between the Generals Halilovic and others in Jablanica. But there was another monitor present. So it was quite some time before that moment in time. So I'm talking about the 25th of April, but I can't really tell you for sure. But you would have to look at the daily reports to be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to another matter, and I would like to turn to a conference that was held on the 18th of April, 1993. Do you recall such a conference?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: 18th of April. You probably mean a conference in West Mostar, in the hospital of West Mostar, but which, if I remember correctly, was followed up by further conversations in Mostar itself close to the headquarters of General Pasalic in an HVO building that changed. The location changed over two days. Then on the 19th or 20th, that was already the day of the departure of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So could you tell us the conference at the hospital in West Mostar on 18th of April, what was the purpose of that conference?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I was not present at that conference, just to say that, and also Mr. Salamanca was not in the conference. CC Mostar and RC Zenica were present. I think there were quite a few people there. I don't think there was any further reason for those people present. As far as I can remember, the subject that was discussed were the usual things. Cease-fire, because in the meantime a great deal of things had happened. So north of Jablanica-Konjic, and in Mostar quite a few things had happened. So it was about cease-fire and a withdrawal of troops or disciplining of troops. Also, free -- it was about free access to middle Bosnia and also the transport of some supplies. I think these were the major issues. Then also minor issues that I didn't really hear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you recall who the participants in this meeting were from Bosnian Croat side?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I shall try using my notes because I forget the time. On the Bosnia side: Mr. Ganic and Mr. -- General Halilovic, and persons accompanying them. On the HVO side: Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, General Petkovic, and accompanying persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned Mr. Ganic, and just to avoid confusion, Mr. Ganic from -- who was he? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ganic -- I have to be careful with the proper name. He was the deputy Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not quite sure about his precise title. A high-ranking official next to President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, you mentioned another person. I didn't quite get that name. I thought the translation came through as Mr. Galilovic [sic]. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: General Halilovic. Yes, he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on that day did you personally have the occasion to speak to any of these people personally, or did they speak to you personally?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I just want to say straight -- straight away that personal conversations were quite rare, just to explain that. When I was in the room in front of the -- of the conference room, then Mr. Prlic came from the outside. He saw me as an ECMM monitor and he talked to me in English. He said, roughly speaking, such an international organisation such as the ECMM didn't have any function, no meaning. Like many other international organisations, it wasn't relevant and he was wondering what we were doing here. We should, rather, go home, he said. It was a bit aggressive, but not very aggressive. Then it turned out that I was German, and then he added that German supported Slovenia and Croatia. They should also support us, Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, that is the -- the community of Herceg-Bosna, and should not ally to the other western states who had something against them, by which he meant Croats or Croatia in general, but I think mainly Herceg-Bosna. But to conclude it, I think, our conversation I only said, "Mr. Prlic, I'm new to this mission, new to the country and I hear what you're saying, but I can also imagine because of my idea of politics, if all this comes to an end, what is happening here, you will certainly need Europe. You might need us." And that concluded our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you had met Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I was told who he was. When he was introduced, where he certainly said his name, then my -- at that moment in time I really didn't catch his name. Only afterwards I knew who he was. It was -- I was told later on it was Mr. Prlic. I think it was by Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you have mentioned a conference which took place around about the 4th or the 5th of May. Could you tell us about this conference, where it took place and what the purpose was?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. On the 4th and 5th of May. Yes, it was a conference that mainly was held in Jablanica in a tent with the Spanish Battalion, but it also took partly place in Mostar and there was a to'ing and fro'ing with the cars. There seemed to be a correlation. I didn't quite catch it because some didn't want to attend the other -- the other occasion. The main conference took place on the 4th and 5th of May in Jablanica in this tent. Do you want me to carry on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: So the main people present at this conference were General Petkovic and General Halilovic, and next to General Petkovic, I assume General Lasic and other HVO soldiers. I forgot. On the Muslim side there was General Pasalic, and on the Muslim side there were so-called brigade commanders. I can remember some of them being present in the room. Among others there was Zuka Nihad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I don't think my learned friend has noticed at line 22, the witness said that Zuka and Nihad were there. The "and" was dropped and now it seems that this is just a single name belonging to one person, whereas in reality these are two different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for my learned colleague. That is indeed correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we could just confirm for the record you mentioned -- is it two people Zuka and Nihad?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. There are two people, two persons. Nihad -- I must always tell you always how people introduce themselves. I can't know it. Zuka was the boss of Nihad. Nihad was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Colonel, the last question that I asked you before this was: What was the main purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a practical attempt by both Generals Halilovic, General Petkovic, to get clarification about the situation in the various areas in Jablanica, Konjic, and Doljani. So not an attempt to do it on -- from one's desk with letters and agreements but to see what we're interested and what we do not know about this region and what -- what do we want to get. But as we were just listening, everything sounded very complicated, so I can't say anything further about it. But I can tell you something about the result. Do you want me to do that? Do you want me to try and do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But I think before we do that, Your Honour, I think it may be the appropriate time to have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing has resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we were talking about the meeting on the 4th of May, which took place in Jablanica, and could you now tell us what was the result of this meeting, what happened as a result thereof?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Although the HVO and then the armija were concerned about their people in Konjic and Jablanica and the northern regions and in Doljani, in particular, it was such, the armija wanted to know what about our people in Doljani. The HVO wanted to know what is up in Kostajnica and in the other towns north of the lake like Novi Straca [phoen] and such places. And the Croatian side wanted to know what about -- what happened after the attacks in Konjic with our Croatian soldiers and the Croatian civil population, Konjic. This was the purpose of the meeting. And for this purpose there were three very strong reconnaissance troops set up to go into the individual regions made up of UNPROFOR, the Spanish Battalion, whatever was available, ECMM, the respective representatives of the HVO and the armija. In each reconnaissance troop, there were people from the armija and HVO soldiers in the Spanish APCs. And the UN officers were there, the UNMOs, the United Nations -- observation officers of the United Nations. For example, I was together with someone from New Zealand. And then the two generals, Petkovic and Halilovic, they said they would go along with each -- or one of these troops. Petkovic would go across the bridge to Kostajnica. Whether this actually took place or not, I don't know, because the entire convoy of this patrol was very long and rather unclear, but I suppose they did. And General Halilovic wanted to go to Doljani, but I can't confirm that. On the ECMM side -- well, I wanted to say also there were also ambulances with us. If injured persons had been found, then they would have been transported off in the ambulances. This was the intention. So there was also -- this was also linked to humanitarian point. In the ECMM, the monitor mission, those present were for the troop to Doljani, Nigel Milverton who represented me on my leave from the 5th of May to the 25th of May, and he was an experienced monitor from other areas. To Konjic there was also a Canadian monitor, and I went in one of the Spanish troop transporters. In -- on this vehicle, apart from the Spanish soldiers, in my immediate proximity there was also, as I mentioned before, the observation officer of the United Nations and Mr. Cibo. This was as far as I know, or as we were told, at least, he was a man -- on the mandate from President Izetbegovic and responsible for the area of Konjic and this wider area. So this was at the beginning. Do you want me to continue my report? Okay. Well, I'll report now on what I saw afterwards in my part. Yes. I said I went to Kostajnica. I think I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And could you tell very briefly what you encountered in your part?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning we had major problems crossing the bridge at Osasac [phoen], because the check-point of the armija didn't want to let us pass. There we had to use our powers of persuasion so that the -- on the part of the armija officers who were travelling with us, but somehow it did work. And then we proceeded very slowly to Kostajnica. And this region around Kostajnica was something which I knew relatively well by the very numerous visits I made in April. So I know Sagolj relatively well, the commander there and others. And the situation was such there was a relatively large number of population on the road, as it was explained to me, Croatian population and I assume that that was true. They were congregated round about the church, and they were afraid, frustrated. They gave the impression of helplessness. Although we then went on further and the aim was, if my pronunciation is correct, to go to Pazaric this is in the north. Pazaric, or something like that, is the name of it. At least, I knew this from the previous day, and this was one of the control points the armija. We didn't actually go there, I can't say why not because I was not at the head of the convoy. We went off to the right and we moved towards the villages as I've mentioned before. Novi Straca, Obrije [phoen], and some others which I really haven't retained in my memory. Then we saw a great deal of destruction in these villages, and I had seen this in part at the end of June, sorry, end of April when I was there already, but this was a series of villages had been destroyed and people were along the road in a state of helplessness. There were telephone lines which had been separated or shot down. And then at some time we were stopped. Somehow or other we couldn't go on. And Mr. Cibo said to his armija people, obviously we have been stopped by armija soldiers, they said that they should let us through because we wanted to reconnoiter the situation or the area. And this was not successful. He was unable to persuade his armija people, and this had to do with some sort of local matter that I didn't really understand, something about dead armija soldiers who should be exchanged or something like this. It was for me an unclear situation. But the result was we turned round the entire convoy, and I was with Cibo at the front of the vehicle. After we turned round the others were behind us. We turned round and we turned along the same road. And the Spanish, the UNMOs, the observation officers of the UN, and myself said that we were presumably in one of these places like Novi Straca. And we saw night was falling and we saw in the twilight human faces behind glass, behind a large glass pane. We got out and we looked at them, and this was obviously a women's prison, for women, children, and elderly people. They were in the building of something similar to a bank. I'd say a bank more, because, as I found out one year later it had been a bank. Otherwise, it would have simply been a low office window with large windows and they were in some sort of room there. We thought there were about a hundred to 150 people there who were in the building in a state of fear. And the children were weeping. We couldn't hear them through the glass but we could see them. We went on, and in Kostajnica, I spoke to Mr. Sagolj whom I knew relatively well from a series of conferences in April. I said, "Mr. Sagolj, you are a soldier. What is going on with those prisoners?" And Sagolj, I would say he wasn't happy in his own skin. He said, however, "I must keep these Muslim people there, the women, children, and elderly people. I hope it's not going to last too long, because the armija has attacked the HVO, has killed HVO soldiers, and has also evacuated Croatian people. If I don't keep them in prison, then I will be killed by my own people, or they will be killed by my own people." And we went back to Jablanica, and the whole matter was concluded there, for me at least. Of course, we reported this to the Red Cross. We made the usual reports, of course. That is a matter of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: A few questions just to clarify a few issues. In the first place, when you refer to Sagolj, who was he specifically?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Sagolj was a brigade commander. I must say, at least this is how they introduced themselves to us and how I got to know him at the time. He was a brigade commander of the -- of a certain brigade in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And for which army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: For the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw a series of villages which were destroyed on the way up during this -- on the travel -- on the first leg of this investigation or trip you made. Do you know which villages those were or who inhabited these villages?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say entire villages but, rather, individual houses, and -- because these houses aren't -- these villages aren't huge. They are only a group of houses. There were some houses, and in these buildings - we knew less of this at the point in time. It was something that was confirmed later - It was mainly Croatian population in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, the place where you saw the women and children being held in the building which later turned out to be a bank, do you know which village this was, or where approximately this village was situated?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I'm relatively sure it was Novi Straca but I can say with this gesture perhaps. It was a bend in the road. The road went like this from east to west and then went up towards the north. And in this corner, it was located there. I can't be more precise than that from my memory, because of course I don't know these places so well from my memory, and I can't recall them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, did anybody else suggest that you also visit this area after you had actually visited this area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: A particular request to go there later, this is something I can't really recall, but it's true, of course, that the -- on the HVO side Mr. Stojic and Mr. Bojic but also other people said to us the ECMM, you must look more closely at the Klis region and not spend so much time in other areas where you think that we Croatians have done something. Don't stay here, but look after us and our compatriots round about this area, round about Jablanica and Konjic. So indirectly but not in concrete terms. This was sort of an ongoing request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I see in the record it says on line 16 of page 42, Mr. Stojic and Mr. Bojic. That Mr. Bojic, that the person that you are referring to, or whom are you referring to specifically? Could it be a Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. That was my mispronunciation. It was Mr. Bozic. I hope my pronunciation is correct now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bozic, who was he, according to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: No. That was simply a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know who he was at that time, what position he --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'd rather talk about his function. There will be no mistake. Mr. Stojic, he was the minister of defence of the HVO, and Mr. Bojic was the deputy defence minister of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic. Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, we may get back to this aspect a bit later on. Just one aspect very quickly. Did you ever speak to anybody during your period as a monitor concerning the question of Mostar as the capital the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was an ongoing subject on the HVO part, but also on the part of the armija, everyone. There was no occasion where this subject did not come up. It always came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Berislav Pusic, when was the first time, if at all, that you met Mr. Berislav Pusic? Could you just tell the Court about that briefly?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him a few times in the conferences, but the first time I'm quite sure it was in Jablanica, although I can't say precisely what -- at what time this was. It must, I think, have been before the conference on the 4th and 5th of May. Round about the end of April. And with many other people we met together in an office building of the electricity works of Jablanica. And in the first meetings, it was to do with a minor point. We had to go somewhere to find something out, and he said no, he wasn't coming with us, or something like that, because there was a -- had been a meeting with armija soldiers, and he didn't want to come with us. So the situation was something like this. It's very difficult for me to reconstruct this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Then, sir, you went on leave to Germany, and if we can focus on when you came back at the end of May. When did you actually travel, according to your recollection and arrive in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I haven't looked up the dates of my journey, but I'm sure that it was the 24th of May, in the evening, I arrived in Siroki Brijeg, and on the 25th, early, I took part in a conference in the west of Mostar. After I'd been away for three weeks this situation was very confusing because of the developments as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what happened on the 25th of -- of May in Mostar? What did you observe specifically on that day?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: The first thing was that I was in this conference that I had previously mentioned, and we were talking about practical things like water supply, electricity supply of East Mostar. This was led by observation officer of the United Nations. I'm really not in a position it say what the results were. Sometimes these discussions remained open without result, so I can't really say. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This conference or the meeting you refer to, who were the other participants or which parties were participating in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: The participants were, although I must be careful here, were civil persons from East and West Mostar whom I can't really describe individually because I think I probably saw them for the first time, at least most of them, so that I can't really give you any further details on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's move on from there and what happened after this conference.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening of the same day, and I thought about it again, it could have also been the evening of the following day. I cannot exclude that completely. It could have been the 26th. Then the other monitor with whom I cooperated and I, we went to West Mostar in one of the main roads which -- perpendicular to the Neretva. It was a kind of theatre close by, or it could have been a cinema as well. Now, I cannot tell you why we went there. There was a rumour, I think, where we got a piece of information that persons were to be exchanged between East Mostar and West Mostar. When we arrived there at about 7.00 p.m., 1900 hours, then we heard, according to rumours that people from East Mostar had come to West Mostar whom I had not seen, however. I can remember that I saw some people arriving by bus. They got off the bus. But I can remember that some of these buses, I think we're talking about five, roughly, were in the direction of Neretva, lined up one after the other, and on these buses there were families, women, children, also elderly people. I did not recognise any men between -- let's say between 16 and 50, who you might have declared to be fighters. And these people looked rather frustrated, unhappy, looked apathetic, looked frightened but indifferent, just -- it was warm. Sometimes doors were opened. Windows were opened in order to get some fresh air. Otherwise, they didn't seem to get any supplies. Nobody looked after them. Some HVO soldiers were guarding these buses, and the man who was -- who look after these soldiers, who was in command, was Mr. Pusic. Mr. Pusic also came towards us and said roughly that was not our business; it was his business, and we should go away. We should move away from the area. We didn't do that. He didn't do it physically, but verbally he told us, "Just leave." We then asked the HVO soldiers and also asked Mr. Pusic and also people who were coming by - occasionally people were going by - what this was all about, and it then emerged to us that these were Muslim families who were transported from East Mostar to West Mostar. It went on until about 2300 hours, and then the buses left in the direction of Neretva. Then we went back to Siroki Brijeg, to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: A few questions. Just for clarity, I don't know if this came out correctly in the record, these people, did they actually get off the bus or stay on the bus when these buses arrived, when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: When we arrived, then they were already on the bus. We did not see them outside of the bus at all. The image, the picture that we had of them were the people on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Furthermore, sir, you say that Mr. Pusic was in command of these HVO soldiers or the soldiers. From what did he say that you say he was in command? What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: First of all, I recognised him again. And also the other monitor knew him. Yes, that could be recognised, the way in which he behaved, like a leader of the few HVO soldiers who obeyed him. He was obviously the leader, the one who said what they should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Mr. Pusic was in uniform or not on that day?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Surprisingly, I can't tell you. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to some exhibits and with the help of the usher if we could perhaps just provide the witness with the exhibit binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the first exhibit that I would refer you to is Exhibit 02557. P 02557. 2557.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: [In English] This document from -- [Interpretation] So the document of the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. It's marked as ECMM restricted, EC monitor mission team report for 29 May. And it is signed by Brad Koskie or in the name of Brad Koskie and Ivan Simovcek. Have you seen this document or do you know of this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I know it and I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to refer you to one aspect of this document, paragraph 1, General situation. It refers in the second line to treatment of the Muslim minority in the south remains in question. If we turn to paragraph 6 the theme continues. "Both UNHCR and ICRC report the internment and eviction of Muslims in Mostar and the towns to the south." And then a few lines down, in the middle of paragraph 6: "The UNHCR and ICRC report that Muslim families on the west bank were evicted last night in organised raids, their homes occupied by Croat families with permits to occupy the flats." My question, sir, is in light of what you saw upon your return, could you comment on this document from that perspective?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: So from the point of view of the ECMM monitors, they're saying what they have heard, learned from others. And the matter that is raised about west bank Mostar in the lower part of paragraph 6, that might refer to what I mentioned before of what happened on the 25th or 26th. Now, whether further such movements happened between the 26th and the 29th in Mostar, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can move on from -- from this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for this section of the witness's evidence, if we could move into private session for about five minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back to open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, upon your return from leave at the end of May, what was the situation for the ECMM regarding access to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: The headquarters of ECMM was still in Siroki Brijeg. The teams with Nigel Milverton at their head reported that in May there was hardly any or practically no access to Mostar. Then at a later stage, I could see that for myself but this was not at the same time when I heard about it but later on when I could go there, what I could see was that the building was where the headquarters of the 4th Corps Armija where General Pasalic was, that this had been partially destroyed. The walls were black because of smoke and -- so the building still existed, but there were major traces of fighting. Also, the outside showed a great deal of traces of fighting. For example, benches had been turned over. You could see some impacts of bullets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did the ECMM at that stage have any problems to go through HVO check-points to enter Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: No problems to access the check-points. No, we didn't have that. I'm talking about the -- I'm not talking about when I wasn't there. We could get to the check-points and then we were told no, along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd quickly like to refer you to two documents concerning activities in June. The first one is Exhibit P 02807. P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please accept my apologies. I find it is a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please answer this question, because I'm under the impression that you answered in a different way as to the check-points. The Prosecutor asked you whether there were -- whether it was possible to enter Mostar, to go through the check-points, and you seem to say yes, on the one hand, and then you say when we would get to the check-points we wouldn't be allowed to go through. So could you be more specific? Was it possible for you to move around freely, and if you could not, why was it not possible to go through the check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The check-points didn't let the monitors go through. That's what I -- that's the report that I got. It said they were told no, you cannot go to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was reported to you. But you yourself, did you encounter any problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of June that I can recollect, I could not get into Mostar because I was also turned down by the check-points. But soon in June, might have been around the 10th of June or something like that, then I went on several occasions to the eastern part of Mostar and the path which -- the path we used, the way we used, was so-called Dam Bridge in the north of Mostar. And then an HVO check-point let us go through. And then on the road to south we went into Eastern Mostar and were in the headquarters of Pasalic on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the exhibit is 2807. 2807.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You have the document before you? Sir --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The title of this document is an ECMM report from Klaus Nissen in Jablanica to the German delegation, headquarters Zagreb, and it's dated the 16th of June, 1993. Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you prepare this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the top, it says from M1, HCC Mostar. Were you HCC Mostar at this stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I was at that time HCC Mostar, and with my team in 1, I worked there immediately because we got some new monitors that I wanted to brief, hence this display here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, just before looking at the contents of the document, just for the record in the bottom right-hand corner there's a signature and a date in October 2002. My first question is: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court when you signed this in October 2002? What occasion was that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: The occasion was that I was asked by the Tribunal to make a written statement about another case, about -- I had already been heard in May 1998 at home, and on that day I went to The Hague and made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That was before an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. In both cases, that is in 1998, which preceded this one, and also in 2002, when I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if we can look at the first paragraph of this document. This deals with negotiations of a team of UNHCR, UNMOs and ECMM members to get four people free. This team went to the entrance of Konjic to meet there the SpaBat. Two platoons and the UNMO who negotiated with a local HVO commander. And then the interesting part: "All negotiations failed, even a fax from Mr. Petkovic, to set the four locals free -- local people free. Did not impress the local HVO commander."
