Could you first tell the Court what was this about, these four people who were mentioned in this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Can I go -- can I go a bit more -- can I tell it in a bit more detail in order to make it more understandable? Near Kostajnica there was a so-called pocket or an HVO enclave in the hills. It was called Konjic pocket or Zabrdje pocket. And so this was a Croat population which was surrounded by, on the one hand, by the Serbs, on the other hand by Muslims, and they stayed there. But at the same time there was the main road leading to Konjic, and there was a check-point and it was closed occasionally. Over and over again when we went to see minorities, we also heard, in that conjunction, we heard about this particular Konjic pocket for various reasons. And none -- nobody of these organisations had been there for weeks or over the past weeks. So we got together and said we're going there. The UN officers from UNMOs arranged this, and I think they arranged it with Sagolj, because as far as I can tell he was also responsible for this pocket with his deputy or one of his leading officers, subordinate officers. It happened, and we agreed upon a date. We then went in the morning with four vehicles of this organisation, ECMM as well, waited for a long time, and then were escorted to the hill, to the mountain, and then saw several small houses which were located on the top of the hills and farmhouses. Then we talked to the commander, and then he informed us there about the population, that wasn't very well of course because they didn't have enough to eat, and they were cut off of all kinds of things. They couldn't move outside the pocket either. It was a very calm conversation. What -- but we had a -- we had some more trouble with -- I'm quite sure it was an HVO military police officer who looked like Rambo, had an ammunition belt. He was quite aggressive, and he wanted to get rid us of as quickly as possible. I do not know the man's name though. Because of his intervention, the visit which had -- was supposed to be a confidence building visit was quite -- was much shorter. And then we pointed out that we wanted to see some prisoners because it was also part of the agreement that we would see some prisoners, that we would go back to Konjic. We would then see prisoners from other areas. So very briefly. It was a matter of minutes. We saw some prisoners in a room which were against -- leaning, sitting against the walls and they didn't look too bad. They looked roughly normal, whatever you mean normal if you're sitting there. They didn't look particularly hard up. But it was just a fleeting visit, just about five minutes, and then we were told to go. But in the meantime I saw the following, and that was so important for me because it was the only time when it happened during my mission. I saw the Serbian soldiers in two vehicles. About six soldiers with Bosnian Serb uniform. I don't want to create any confusion here, with a hat, caps, and also marks on their vehicles. They put boxes on their vehicles. There could have been ammunition there, also supplies, food supplies, troop supplies -- food, tins with food. So they put several boxes on the vehicle. We didn't have contact with them, but it was interesting to me because it was the only time where I saw Serb, Croat soldiers from Bosnia-Herzegovina. We then left quickly and we were escorted down the mountain. And after about 500 metres, there was massive firing from the front and the rear. The convoy was stopped and we were forced to leave the vehicles, and we were herded together, about 18 people, 16 to 18 people, and we were more or less herded together because of the shooting. No one was injured, and no one was immediately hit, but there was shooting round about us and into the earth. We sat in a kind of bush alongside the road, and we sort of cowered down beside this bush. And it was the soldiers round about us that were relatively calm and we thought they were grinning to themselves because of this overall situation, as if it was a pre-planned action and "We want to show them," but the leader of this group seemed to us to be extremely frustrated personally. He was highly aggressive, and you couldn't see any grin on his face. We had to assume that at any time it could be a matter of life and death. Then we said those we recognised as native inhabitants, we wanted to find out who they were. There were four Muslims, four men and a woman, an interpreter, who had to separate themselves from us, and we tried to intervene and say, No, we're not going along with that. And so they shot into the bushes in front of us so that we were afraid, and we thought that this -- these tactics would not work out. Maybe somebody would be injured. So we separated from the others, and then they said to us, "You disappear with your vehicles and those four, they stay here," and that's what happen. We drove down the mountain, and at the bottom we consulted, deliberated on this. We went to the Spanish Battalion, and then the whole reporting business started to the HVO, the armija, to Zagreb and others to say that they really should look after these people who had been taken prisoner. Do you want me to continue my report? Because this comes into another phase. But this was the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And tell us about how you obtained the fax from Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, if I recall, I didn't receive a fax personally from Mr. Petkovic, but I know in this case through UNMOs or the Spanish Battalion, I have to say this is secondhand, that General Petkovic sent a fax to his people in the pocket saying that these prisoners should be released immediately. And this was on the same day, and obviously this didn't happen on the same day because they said no. Why I'm saying so clearly they said no is based on another source which I only received a few days later. It was a handwritten letter from this pocket, from the people there, but at least from the leader there, saying that "we have taken them prisoner because no one is bothering about us. We are alone. We will be rubbed off and no one will be bothered with us any more. There was not," and this was a decisive point, "there was not this support from our own people. No one is bothering about us, neither the Herceg-Bosna nor Croatia." This was the line going through the fax. "So we had to resort to our devices." This was the summary. And this basically confirmed our previous impression of isolation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if you say, "they said no," this is to the release of these people. Who do you refer to by "they"?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, you mean who was released, or perhaps I haven't quite understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No. My question is if you say, "they said no," who is "they" that refused you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: No. I wasn't actually quoting, but I'm saying this was the result of what I've -- I've just summarised, is the result of what the commander said. But I tried to put it in the context that I can only say this explicitly in terms of Mr. Petkovic, because I didn't know this actually on the very day. On that day I didn't know that Mr. Petkovic had written this letter. This was something which emerged later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How was the release of these people eventually obtained, these four people?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Then in the night of that day and the following morning, there were various links. The International Red Cross had intervened, for example, with Mr. Pogarcic in Grude. Contact was made and there were many other contacts especially to Mr. -- or certainly to Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic, presumably, and the other deputy defence minister. And then I heard of SpaBat. This is not my personal knowledge, that General Petkovic, with a SpaBat armoured vehicle, had tried to get to Jablanica and then to Konjic to release those hostages, to convince his people on site. And he failed according to the Spanish Battalion because the armija check-points south of Jablanica, in Dreznica, further to the south, didn't let him through. Obviously, the verbal pressure, however this was built up, I don't know the details, led to the situation that they relented and the Spanish Battalion received a report that they could drive to this place on the road before Konjic and fetch these four people, which they did. This took place on the late afternoon or the early evening of the following day. These people were uninjured. They were completely clothed. They had all their money on them. Nothing had been taken from them, and they had been treated properly. The men said they had been slightly threatened, but they said that it wasn't really serious. And the young lady who was with them said that they behaved correctly. And then they were taken by the Spanish Battalion, taken back to Jablanica and back to their colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the document, and it's the end of -- or it's about the fifth or sixth line in paragraph 1 where it says: "The fax from Mr. Petkovic to get the four local people free did not impress the local HVO commander." From your experience of this situation and your knowledge, can you comment on how this reflects, if at all, on Mr. Petkovic's ability to exert authority?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this says little about his authority, because I know from other situations, because leaders who are not confronting those they are leading eye-to-eye really don't much opportunity of having their commands carried out. I must say this in all clarity because there was a lack of confidence whether the order was correct or not. It was questioned. Perhaps someone else gave the order and used his name. What they people -- they up there know about us? If they knew how we were doing, then they would never have issued the order. So there are many pros and contras, but basically this really doesn't say much about his authority. On the contrary. You could seen say that he was obviously aware of this fact because he had tried to intervene personally. He knew the interpretation that I had given. He probably knew this better than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if we can step off this document, and if we can look at document 2947. 2947. That's exhibit -- the very next one. Exhibit P 02947. This document says from ECLO Kiseljak. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My first question is: Do you know what ECLO stands for?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the abbreviation for the liaison officer of the ECMM at the headquarters of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak. European Community Liaison Officer. This is the English title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this document is dated the 25th of June, 1993, and it is addressed to various instances but also to CC Mostar. Now, would that have been to your team on the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And as a matter of routine, we received such reports as Kiseljak received reports from Zenica as a matter of routine. And we can say that unless there were technical difficulties, we received these reports and used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can refer you to paragraph 7(B). Paragraph 7 deals with the SpaBat sector. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, 7(B) deals with Mostar, and what I would like to refer to is the third bullet under that, the very end of the page. "During one of the clashes, one Muslim girl was wounded through the shooting of HVO snipers." My question to you is at this time, this is towards the end of June 1993, were you aware of sniping taking place in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: In -- this individual case is one that I don't know from the report, but I know of the snipers in Mostar who targeted East Mostar more and more, rather than by reverse, because I personally witnessed such shootings. Not aimed at us, but as I reported in June, even -- in June when I visited the command post of Pasalic, sometimes there was more shooting, sometimes less, sometimes none at all, and sometimes the bullets impacted the building and the plaster fell off the walls. But I didn't experience mortar firing. In June there was a team of the UN -- the English term is the -- well, to the observers of the initially -- or of the UN was in Mostar and had moved into quarters in the east part of Mostar, and we visited them of course too and it was rather courageous of them to move up there and they barricaded the house with wood and they used the rooms in the cellar rather than rooms on the first floor. And they weren't targeted particularly, but often snipers were out there and they had reported of grenades and mortar shells, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can briefly refer you to - in line with what you've just said now - Exhibit 2658. 2658. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report dated the 7th of June, 1993. It's an ECMM team report, and it's in the name of Brad. Have you seen this report previously? Do you know of it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'd like to refer to is simply paragraph 8, the second sentence. "UNMO have deployed a team to the east bank of Mostar on a permanent basis." And my simple question is when you say that you experienced sniping in the UNMO location or base on the -- in East Mostar, how does this relate to what we read in paragraph 8, "UNMO have deployed a team to the east bank"?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: UNMO wanted to observe the particular situation in East Mostar. We, for example, the first time we wouldn't have been able to do so without approval, but we were bound to refrain from night operations, and we weren't out at night unless by chance. But they, from their headquarters, were able to observe the entire situation over a number of days, and this is why they were particular witnesses, because they were at the top of the mountain and they experienced every single shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if we can step off that document and -- actually, if we can very briefly return to the previous document, 2947. 2947.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if we can turn to paragraph 7 once again. Now, we have -- we've looked at 7(B). If we can turn the page and go to 7(C), and there we see Jablanica-Konjic. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The fifth bullet under that: "According to ECMM reports they saw one video with killed HV soldier, ID card from special forces of Croatia." I don't want to ask you about that specific incident. My simple question to you is did you as an ECMM officer have any specific instructions regarding HV presence in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, in fact from the very beginning there was a general mandate to have the borders between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, we should observe this to see if there were movements of troops. There was a particular instruction about the end of June, the beginning of July of this year when there were uprisings, we'll come back to that, I think, of the armija in the north of Mostar, maybe in the south as well there was such uprising. And we assumed from Zagreb that this could be the reason to bring Croatian troops into Bosnia. So there was a particular mandate to observe the border and to take every opportunity to go to the border and to keep our eyes open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if we can turn to the end of June. On the 30th of June, 1993, the Court has heard that the ABiH launched an attack to the North Camp in Mostar. Were you aware of that attack?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. On the 13th of June we found out about these events, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to document 3069. 3069.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You have the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, that is ECMM report for the 1st of July, 1993, and it's in the name of Brad and Christ. Do you know of this report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 3 of this report dealing with meetings, it's reported that "The meeting with brigade commander Colonel Obradovic was cancelled. We were not allowed through the HVO check-point en route to his headquarters approaching Stolac. Specific orders were given barring the ECMM and other international agencies." My first question was did you know who Colonel Obradovic was?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I had never seen Colonel Obradovic myself, but I knew of him from the very beginning. From the beginning of April, he was the brigade commander in - I don't want to confuse the places - in Capljina. In the south of Capljina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm not absolutely sure of the place, but I think it was the south of Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, can you comment on the fact that he had cancelled a meeting on the day after the attack on the North Camp? Was there a link, do you know?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: On the 1st of July when this report arrived I could conclude from the general picture as to why this had happened, why this report was set up, because on the 30th of June, late afternoon, we learnt from various sources that single soldiers, probably also some troops, parts of troops, but, rather, single soldiers of the armija who served under the HVO had risen against the HVO, against their leaders, and there had been shootings. And also losses on both sides had occurred. There were dead -- dead people or injured -- also, people were injured among the civilian population. At least in the north. I don't know about the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the final paragraph or sentence that I -- that I've read to you already in that first bit under paragraph 3: "Specific orders were given barring ECMM and other international agencies." And if we can turn from there perhaps to the assessment at the bottom, paragraph 6. "Preparations are being made for a counter-offensive and the world is not invited to watch." Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: It's not easy, but from the information that I personally got of the 30th of June, I could assume that at any rate the HVO, because of the uprising on the 30th of June reacted vehemently. As to what that was like in single incidents whether you can talk about counter-offensive, whether you can see it quite like that or whether it was just a local reaction, I cannot tell you. At least at this moment in time. Later on the whole matter took quite a different direction though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From this time onwards, so the 30th of June, the 1st of July onwards, what was the situation of the ECMM regarding access to Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: After this date we no longer had access to Mostar, and I'm sure I personally never went to Mostar again until the 25th or 26th of July, when I finished the mission. A lot of attempts were made, and a lot of discussions took place, also at a level above my level, that is with Zagreb, and people who were on the -- on location with Mr. Bruno Stojic and also Mr. Bozic, we -- attempts were made to gain access. There were discussions at a later stage but it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can refer you to the next document in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we go to that, if we could make sure that we get the name of the second individual for the record. Page 66, he mentioned two names. On line 25, he mentioned two particular names and I don't believe that it was caught because we have new interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, yes, if you could perhaps help. The names I heard, the first one Mr. Bruno Stojic, and then another person.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Maybe I mispronounced it. Maybe I'm going to mention his function. The deputy defence minister of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that be Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I always thought that these -- that there was a little hook on the z, but it seems to be wrong. Maybe that's the right pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you to my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the very next exhibit in the binder is 3162. Exhibit 3162. And this is a handwritten note or letter titled "Protest. Regarding freedom of movement ECMM," and it's dated the 3rd of July, 1993, addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic. Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I have also signed it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who wrote the document itself? Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was written by the other monitor who worked in this function. It was Toon van der Grinten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just before looking at the document, you mentioned when you returned on the 25th in West Mostar, when you saw the five buses with people on them, that you were with a colleague. Which colleague was that at that stage? I omitted to ask you previously.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was the same one who also wrote this document, Mr. van der Grinten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if Mr. van der Grinten, if he wrote this, did he also compose the letter or was that composed in a different manner, the content?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: We did -- we did the wording together, and he was the one who was writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, did he write it in English or in B/C/S, that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the original text that he wrote down, as he wrote it down, and it was translated into Serbo-Croat by our translator and both letters are handwritten by Mr. van der Grinten and the translator and then were sent off by fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, we've been looking at the English document. If we turn the page there is a second document, also handwritten. Is this the handwritten version you refer to that was translated?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, this is the translated version. I have to make sure that I don't get the papers confused. It could also be another text, but it is the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we look at the first paragraph of this letter, in the third line, well, second line, "... On 12 May 1993 we strongly protest against restricting the ECMM team Mostar to enter the city. Three days 'Team Mostar' tried to contact Mr. Stojic without success." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Just to be sure, you're talking about the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. It's as contained in your -- sorry, it's -- sorry. Just to remove all doubt, I may be misleading or confusing the Court. This is a reference to a memorandum of understanding signed on 1 October at Sarajevo, and the agreement signed on 12 May 1993. "We strongly protest," and then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: So this document of the 12th of May, this is an agreement that we concluded and that we signed. It was the Generals Halilovic and Petkovic, and General Morillon from France, and the head RC Zenica, Mr. Thebault. And then several paragraphs are mentioned. From memory, I can say there was talk about cease-fire, a transfer of troops, freedom of movement of international organisations, as well about transports to -- with access to middle Bosnia, if I recollect correctly. This was the document, and this was a high-level document. You might say that that should have been quite important, but I'm putting that into question by the way I'm saying this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, tell us about what happened regarding this letter, whether any steps were taken, whether there was any result to this letter that you sent.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I myself haven't seen any results, and I don't think other people either, and the people concerned didn't see any either. At least at a later meeting which I think took place on the 18th of May on a higher political level, there were the Generals Halilovic and Petkovic or Pasalic, I'm not quite sure who was concerned, they also conceded that their order of the agreement of the 12th of May, which had then been translated into orders, that it didn't have any effect. That was their own statements. I read this in the minutes, possibly in some of the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a good time for a break perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, just before the break we were still looking at the letter of protest that you had sent to Mr. Bruno Stojic on the 3rd of July, 1993. In this letter if we look at the second paragraph, towards the end it says: "We like to meet Mr. Stojic in person or any other high-ranking authority who can give us that important information." Did anything come of this? Was there any subsequent meeting to this letter of protest?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Afterwards there was a first meeting on the 5th of July between the minister of defence and myself, and interpreters and so on. And afterwards on the 10th and 11th of July there were meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The meetings of the 10th and the 11th of July, with whom were those meetings?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: They took place with the minister of defence and the deputy minister of defence on the one hand and representatives from Zagreb from the ECMM, from the headquarters in Zagreb, in particular the then-Belgian General Pioge, and the deputy for military operations Colonel Ford, and also the RC Zenica was represented by Mr. Thebault, at least for part of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to the first meeting which you refer to on the 5th of July. Was that with Mr. Stojic himself?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That took place between Mr. Stojic and myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: The meeting took place in a hotel restaurant in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what transpired or what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic put forward very many arguments to tell me why at the time he did not want international organisations and ECMM, to let these organisations into Mostar. There were many other things. Mr. Bruno Stojic at the time outlined the situation of the 30th of June. That is when the Muslims had this uprising, as we talked about. That was one point. And then he said that because of the uprising of the armija soldiers, the HVO was weakened. He didn't admit it, that they were weakened, but this was something that you could derive from the context, that the HVO was in a difficult situation and were annoyed. He also confirmed that in the south, in the area of Branovic that we talked about before, to the south -- or perhaps that was the wrong name, but in the south of Mostar soldiers were -- took place in an uprising and it was said that the HVO had taken many armija soldiers prisoner, and consequently the HVO was weakened on two counts. On the one hand they had lost soldiers from their own ranks and, secondly, they had to look after these prisoners. So the HVO had lost combatants at that time. And from a military point of view, I don't want to talk about other political issues in this context, but they had to take measures to master the situation again, to fight the armija and to defend themselves against the armija and to make sure that they had supplies and provisions looking at it from a purely military point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Stojic's position regarding the ECMM access to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: At least he admitted that there was basic justification. He did not deny this, because on the basis of this -- these documents, but he said our security would not be guaranteed sufficiently in Mostar and at the moment he could not guarantee this. He then said possibly he could bring an ECMM team together with an escort into his office to discuss something or to look at the situation there. But this did not take place either. What is questionable is if it had come about would this have been any use? Because the intention was not to come into the office by direct means. We then could have stayed in Siroki Brijeg, but it did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Colonel, did you respond to the position of Mr. Stojic that the reason you didn't have access was for your own safety or to protect you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: We -- or I, of course, said to him that we are prepared and willing if we have an armoured vehicle to look after our own protection, and understandably enough he pointed out the MOU and the document of the 12th of May and said from his point of view the security of international organisations is described here, or it is ordered here, and he could not relinquish his duty simply on my order. I think in diplomatic terms that was correct. So there was no success.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can refer you to Exhibit 3196. 3196. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is an ECMM daily summary for the 5th of July, 1993, and if we look at paragraph 2, it says: "Political activity. When we met HVO MOD Bruno Stojic..." And my question is: Is this the report on the meeting that you had that we've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: What I said -- these are my recollections on this text which reflects more precisely what was said because it was precise at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we just look at the last page of this document, it says, "Best regards, HCC Mostar and The Flying Dutchman." HCC Mostar is you. Who is The Flying Dutchman?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, it's perhaps not according to the book, but this is a Dutch monitor. I can't give you his name spontaneously. I know it of course, but I have to think about it. I don't have it on the tip of my tongue. It was The Flying Dutchman but it was not according to the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 1 of this document, "General situation," then we see the second paragraph as it were: "On local radio -- on local radios, HVO has done several announcements concerning that soldiers should go to their units, money should be given to support the country. Soldiers still living in other areas should come to serve the HVO. And then there's talk of a curfew. Closing of most of the shops and restaurants has been announced again." At this time or during your time as a monitor, were you aware of the radio being used as a medium to communicate with people in the area where you were a monitor?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was something that we were aware of on several counts. And from the text, you see that there are these inverted commas. This is an original quotation because, amongst other things, one of our interpreters who worked for us was an employee of the radio in Siroki Brijeg, and this report refers to the radio in Siroki Brijeg. I don't know about other transmission stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The last sentence of that paragraph says: "For HVO there is a serious situation." Can you comment on what is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. What is meant is what I mentioned in another context, that is on -- because of the uprising, the armija soldiers and the consequences, the HVO was in a very difficult situation at the moment, and they didn't have the superiority which presumably they had had before in the area of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can step off this document. If we can look at Exhibit 3175. Exhibit 3175. Do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a daily report from the ECMM, and it is dated the 4th of July, 1993, and it is in the name, at the end, of Brad. This document, do you know of this or have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: To recognise it again I would have to read parts of it, but I think I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I will refer you to a specific part, and that is paragraph 6. Now, if we bear in mind this is the day before the meeting you had with Mr. Stojic regarding ECMM access, paragraph 6 says: "Other points: Colonel Obradovic gave his account of the current conflict." And then a few lines down: "In response to the perceived internal threat, all Muslim members of the HVO under his command have been removed. The shortages have been made up by the general mobilisation. In addition, all Muslim males between the ages of 18 and 60 within the Capljina municipality and the villages of -- south of Mostar have been arrested. This involves military and civilian police." Can you comment in general on this. Were you aware of these activities taking place?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I can't say that so precisely because I don't know these places individually, but it was basically south of the line of Buna-Blagaj. This was the line where the armija and the HVO were confronting each other. And I would like to point out briefly there was a document at the beginning of May from General Pasalic saying clearly that he was aware of the fact that many soldiers of the armija had collected in the area of the line I mentioned up to Metkovic. Perhaps not quite so far to the south, but he was very well aware of this fact. The other side were aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Have a look at the third last paragraph of paragraph 6. It's at the top of the next page, on the second page of the document. And that is the sentence which -- which states: "Colonel Obradovic stated that restrictions to movement were done for our safety and could be expected to be lifted very soon." This sounds pretty much like what Mr. Stojic told you the next day. Do you have any comments on that paragraph, on that sentence?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know precisely his opinion, but I think he referred to his area of operations as a soldier, although the ECMM team, as far as I recall, only once or in one of the following days experienced some restriction within his scope of command. So things were relatively good as far as access was concerned. Perhaps from other reports I may have had, we can come back to that, from SpaBat they were subject to more stringent restrictions and that they were able to move about unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to Exhibit 3221. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This document, dated the 6th of July, 1993. It's an ECMM report, R3 to RC Zenica, and it's in the name of Brad and Peter. In the second paragraph, there is political activity reported referring to Mr. Markovic, mayor of Capljina. Do you recognise this document? Had you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the second paragraph on political activity, this deals with the Cap Anamur, refugee camp, and it deals with the freeing of refugees from that camp. Were you aware of that situation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew of the camp personally. Not at this point in time but previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What is being reported here about the closure of the camp? Did you gain any knowledge of what was happening at this period of time? Perhaps if we -- if we just look a bit further down. My apologies. Referring to the removal of these Muslims from the camp, in the middle of that paragraph: "The mayor insisted on statements that were leaving voluntarily and for proper forms to be filled out." And further down: "The forms are to prevent this accusation, and that is that there is a concern that the municipality of Capljina will be accused of ethnic cleansing." Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I can say that the International Red Cross, above all, was always in an ambiguous situation. On the one hand they wanted to help people. They wanted to help them to come and to go into safe areas. For example, there was the question of moving them to Germany and a wagon camp, but on the other hand the International Red Cross was immediately then criticised, that is, that they would support ethnic cleansing or the transfer of people. So the mayor, Markovic, takes up again this kind of reasoning, this argumentation, because at this moment in time it's not ethnic cleansing, it's a voluntary movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was your own view on the voluntariness of this movement, if you are in a position to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: If whatever, if pressure is exerted, if then persons are being harmed physically and psychologically in single incidents, if people are being treated badly or even killed, then in my opinion then such pressure mounts up for the larger community that you can no longer talk about voluntary movements no matter how this is actually done. So that applies to all areas in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can move to another document, the very next document in the binder or exhibit, 3223. Exhibit 3223. Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This document is from ECLO, European Community Liaison Officer Kiseljak, and it's dated. It's a daily information summary for the 6th of July, 1993. Would you have received this in the normal course of events?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can turn to paragraph 6 of this document. And that is the paragraph which starts with "SpaBat sector." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Next paragraph, 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This paragraph says: "The fighting continued in Mostar and Jablanica-Konjic area. HVO started to arrest ... People through the whole area." And on the next page, the second bullet, "HVO is arresting Muslim civilian people as well as trying to disarm the Muslims still enlisted in its units." Do you have any comments to add to this about what you had already perhaps said regarding the previous document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Basically, no. I think, first of all, the Muslim soldiers were arrested that were deemed to be the perpetrators or the ones who had staged the uprising or people who had been in hiding, who hadn't declared themselves openly so that further investigation were carried out, and then further arrests were being made. That might be a possible explanation. As far as the civilian persons are concerned, I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to the next exhibit. It's the next exhibit in the binder as well, 3278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, regarding the last document, can you please go to paragraph 6, item (4) in this paragraph. It is stated that the new commander of the 41st Brigade of the ABiH in Mostar is Semir Dublic Lovac, a former commander of the ABiH snipers in Mostar. Can you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can see the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have information as to the fact that the new person in charge of the 41st Brigade was a former commander of the ABiH snipers or is that something that you are discovering? That's just the way I do now on reading this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not aware of that, hasn't didn't -- I haven't been aware of that fact, and I don't know the name either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the next document or exhibit was 3278. It's the next one in the binder. Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And once again, this is a European Community Liaison Officer Kiseljak, daily information summary for 7 July 1993. Would you have received this document as well?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can once again turn to paragraph 6. It seems that the structure of all these reports is pretty much the same. The relevant paragraph will always be paragraph 6. "SpaBat sector." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look at (B), the third bullet: "Reports about people inside a tunnel used as an ammo store by the JNA in Dretelj," but I assume that's a misspelling of Dretelj. This stage or perhaps subsequently, had you heard about a tunnel in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I have heard rumours about such a tunnel and people being in it. Also, previously, but I haven't seen this tunnel personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The fourth bullet -- sorry, the fifth bullet refers to, "According to BiH sources, 6.000 Muslims were arrested in the Heliodrom." Are you aware of that or do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Again, there were rumours or indications or people -- or talks about it, but nothing tangible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if we can move to the very next exhibit in the binder. That is 3298. And this is once again European Community Liaison Officer Kiseljak, daily information summary for the 8th of July, 1993. Would you have received this report too?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just at this stage, do you know from what information the information contained in these reports was compiled?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I can only something very basic because it always happened like that. The liaison officer received his information from an UNPROFOR unit in Kiseljak, plus the observations of the UN observers. And on occasions, and we also did this, they used reports that came in from other international organisations. So that applies to that report as well as to other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to paragraph 6 of that report once again, "SpaBat sector." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I've just seen the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That was "SpaBat sector."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: (B) "Mostar," and if we look at paragraph or bullet (1) at least. "All UNPROFOR movement on entering the city is still restricted." On this date did this -- was this also applicable to other international organisations apart from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether it applied totally to everyone or whether exceptions were being made but, basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if you say "yes", what do you mean by "yes"? Sorry. Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: So the access to Mostar was barred to everyone. I just want to exclude that there might be an exception about which I do not know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: So single vehicles for -- of the International Red Cross. I just gave an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to Exhibit 3361. 3361. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: No. 3361. I'm not sure -- 3298; is that correct? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a misunderstanding. I thought you were also referring to the numbering of the old report, and this is we're talking -- I have you've got the new report in front of me now. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake. This exhibit is once again European Community liaison officer Kiseljak, daily information summary for 10 July, 1993, and as with the others, would this report have come to you as well?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to paragraph 6 once again. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, "SpaBat sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And then if we turn to (C) "Mostar" at the bottom of that page, and this reports then on the 10th of July, "All UNPROFOR movements in the area of responsibility, particularly in the HVO-controlled areas are even more restricted." Could you comment on this and perhaps also from the point of view of ECMM access?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I assume that what they mean is that the freedom of movement of the Spanish Battalion south of Mostar because they had their command post in Medjugorje, and there was their troops there and they had to go back to Medjugorje so that they had the freedom of movement within that area. This is my assumption. As far as ECMM is concerned, I can only reiterate it's only -- there was only a single incident that I recall because I was also in that place where next to Medjugorje there was a crossroads that was barred, and you couldn't just go across but you were directed onto the left-hand side. There was a barrier but only for a short spell of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we look at the second bullet: "It is believed that the HVO has arrested hundreds of civilians, so they do not want witnesses. Local Muslim sources claimed that." On the next page: "All Muslims in the Capljina-Stolac area have been expelled from their homes and most of them are now imprisoned in Dretelj and Gabela." My question is, was the ECMM able to gain access to these areas to see or verify any of these things being reported at that stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: As far as the report of the ECMM at that moment in time are concerned, I can't really say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to the next document. The next exhibit would be Exhibit 3346. Do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document entitled, "Agreement on the passage of humanitarian convoys." And it appears that this document comes from round about the 10th of July, 1993. Were you aware of such an agreement being concluded?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I only learned about it afterwards, that is, after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We see in -- in this document on the third page there's a list of people who attended -- there's a list of people who attended the meeting. It says: "For the Croatian Defence Council, Dr. Jadranko Prlic." Are you in a position to comment on his authority regarding matters such as these, humanitarian convoys, to conclude such an agreement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I think he was authorised to conclude such an agreement, because he was the head, as I might call him, of the HVO, and it concerned the HVO as a whole, politically and militarily, to agree to such convoys to the north, to middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like to focus your attention on two matters which will be relevant for the next few documents, other documents we may be looking at. Paragraph 6 of this document. That's on the second page, paragraph 6. Do you have it? Paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: -- says that "The representatives of the Croatian Defence Council and the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in there respective areas of responsibility, without stopping and controlling, guarantee the movement of humanitarian convoys." And then paragraph 9. Once again the same two parties, the HVO and the ABiH: "... Shall assure the unhindered passage for all international humanitarian convoys as well as convoys of non-governmental organisations ..." Just before stepping off this document, are you aware or after this agreement was concluded, to your knowledge was there unrestricted access for humanitarian convoys to all areas which would have been covered by this agreement, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, my area of responsibility I can say that these convoys would have to go through Mostar, through west or east, and that didn't take place. I repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I've got music in my ears. Thank you. Sorry, we just had music in our ears for a moment.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat? Do you want me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Perhaps just for safety, yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: So in my area of responsibility, such convoys had to go through the main link through Mostar, and that certainly didn't happen, as you can very well imagine, or as you know straight away. Also, not through Jablanica and Konjic. Another route went through from Grude to north, Tomislavgrad via the mountains, et cetera. Such convoys always played an important role, and if there had been a breakthrough, a decisive breakthrough, then I would have learned about it. But when my successor arrived and when I briefed him, Sir Martin Garrod, which was almost at the end of my time, 23rd of July, roughly, then we went to Zenica, and then we went to -- through Puzel [phoen], and then on this trek through the mountains we saw vehicles who were driving north, roughly speaking. But whether this can retrace back -- can be traced back to such a document, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: One final thing on this document. If we turn to page 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The second -- the two last lines there, or the second last line, it says that for the government of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Mate Granic, was also present. Could you provide any comment as to why the Republic of Croatia would be involved in such an agreement such as this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, for the opening of the supply routes it was necessary to drive through Croatia at the -- starting from the port of Ploce and possibly also using airports, and this was areas under Croatian sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let's turn to Exhibit 3410. Exhibit 3410. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Not at the moment. I'm still looking. Now I have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report or a document from CC Mostar, dated the 12th of July, 1993. And if we see in the subject heading: "Special report concerning the meeting with General Pioge and COO Colonel Ford with deputy minister of defence, HVO, Mr. Bozic. 11 July in Siroki Brijeg. Also present, Klaus Nissen HCC Mostar." Do you recall or have you seen this document, first of all?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The meeting which is reported on -- in this document, do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, from our point of view, first of all the question had to do again with the access to Mostar, and this was subsequent to the protest to the minister of defence. It was all seen in a temporal context. Furthermore, because of the visit of the higher staff from Zagreb, the invitation, of course, went to the minister of defence and the deputy minister of defence to meet these people to discuss the situation in general terms, and he accepted this invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, COO, just for the record, would that stand for chief operations officer or something else?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look -- in this document we see that Mr. Bozic, in paragraph 4, was asked, and this is the fourth last line of paragraph 4: "... Asked Bozic if he could help in ensuring free movement for international agencies." Do you recall what the reaction of Mr. Bozic was?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Well, whether he gave a different answer to that we heard from the minister of defence or not is something I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can we just look at the very last paragraph, paragraph 11 on the last page. "In spite of three separate attempts during a two and a half hour meeting to persuade him to give the answer on the question of freedom of movement, Bozic did not respond at all." Can you perhaps just comment on that. Do you have anything further to add to that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: No. I think he had agreed with the minister of defence and again said if the opportunity occurs and if it fits in with our considerations then we could do something with an escort to start with, but I can't say any more on the score.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's turn to Exhibit 3427. It's just the next document in the -- in the binder. Exhibit 3427. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, once -- or this is a document from CC Mostar, so an ECMM daily summary for the 13th of July, 1993, and at the top it says: "Including DR and M9." Who is M9?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: This abbreviation M9 was used by us for the head of CC Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And would that have been you at that stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know of this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Under "Political activity," we see "HCC and designated HCC Mostar." It starts with that. HCC would be you then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who was designate -- designated HCC at that stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was Sir Martin Garrod, who, if I may add, at this particular point in time did report for me because his English, of course, was much better than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So the first paragraph where we have just started says that you and Sir Martin Garrod, then, "Today had a meeting with Mr. Zubak, vice-president of HVO in the ECMM house in Siroki Brijeg." Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The very next paragraph: "Mr. Zubak explained that the UNHCR meeting in Makarska, a protocol had been signed following the 10th of May protocol." My question on that. Does this refer to the agreement that we have just looked at about 10 minutes ago on humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. He meant this agreement with this, and there was a sort of precursor of Makarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you mean with Mr. Zubak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: This meeting? Well, to give you some more information, since June there was a comparatively closer cooperation between CC Mostar, without taking sides here, with the vice-president Zubak. He came to us repeatedly -- or we saw each other repeatedly. And the first reason for this was to stick to this tradition, and Sir Martin Garrod was to be introduced to Mr. Zubak. And so we had a general political discussion, talked about the current situation. So it was a visit of politeness, first of all, and from that we took part in lengthier conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the first page, the very last line. "Mr. Zubak said that in the moment when there is the fighting, ECMM cannot do anything, but they are very important. Then there is a little chance of peace. And then he invited us to see him and Mr. Prlic as soon as possible -- as soon as it could be possible in his office in Mostar." Can you perhaps just comment on this portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I'm relatively sure that it was not only a matter of politeness. It could appear to be so. But this was his inner conviction, that things had to move on once the war is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's have a look, then, in light of what you say at the assessment, paragraph 8. The same document, at the bottom. And the last half assessment it says: "The main idea of Mr. Zubak to see ECMM today could have been not to lose contact because ECMM are cut off from information now but may be needed in the future. The offer to meet Mr. Prlic is an additional indication of that." Can you add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. This corresponds to what I just said. I can't add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's -- ah. Before we move to another exhibit, Mr. Zubak, did you have any other meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: He was present at meetings, as far as there were, in Medjugorje in May and then in June, and beyond that, in comparison with other political figures, we had regular meetings, maybe five, six meetings with him personally in Siroki Brijeg. And to repeat myself, without taking sides, for a short period of time this was almost like his office. Because of the development in the federation afterwards, it was justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you say, "this was almost like his office", are you referring to the ECMM office in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Earlier today you made mention of an incident with Mr. Demirovic. Can you tell us about that and in the context of your dealings with Mr. Zubak? Perhaps starting off with when this was.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: A meeting with Mr. Demirovic. Now, I must be careful with the date. I think it was at the end of May, but I'm not absolutely sure. But I think it was the end of May. And this took place in Siroki Brijeg, in an inn, and the head of RC Zenica was there, Mr. Thebault, Mr. Zubak, an interpreter, and myself. And Mr. Demirovic whose name had been known to us for some time, he had been appointed by Izetbegovic, or commissioned, so to speak, because I don't know exactly what his position was, but he had the responsibility for the area, Mostar in particular. It might have expanded towards the north, but there were various rumours as to where he might be. He couldn't be found, he was in hiding, he was in prison, and so on. And in this case I talked to Mr. Zubak several times about it because we could talk relatively openly with each other, and he organised this meeting on that account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And during the meeting with Mr. Demirovic, did the aspect of the safety of the family of Mr. Demirovic, was that discussed?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Demirovic said that so far his wife and daughter, as far as I recall, had not been pestered. That is, his son was in another prison and probably in Ljubuski, presumably. And he had asked us, therefore, to release him but at least to treat him correctly. And then Mr. Zubak, as far as I remember, said, without looking at the document again, "We'll look into it, and I will ask Mr. Pusic to make sure."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you take stage -- did you take stage know who Mr. Pusic was already?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. At that point I did know, although the distribution of the actual task was something I wasn't sure about. Sometimes it was about displaced persons. Sometimes it was prisoners of war, sometimes refugees. So it wasn't quite clear how sharply delineated this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After this meeting do you know whether anything further happened regarding this matter, the release of Mr. Demirovic's son?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zubak at a later point in time explained that release at that point was not possible. Presumably he had talked to other members of the government. He had been designated vice-president, and this shows that Mr. Zubak, perhaps it don't appear so, that he of course quite clearly had the interests of his own citizens in mind, and he kept track of it. And I've found indications in other areas I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to the next exhibit in the binder which is Exhibit 3453. Exhibit 3453. Do you have it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is a further European Community Liaison Officer Kiseljak, information or daily situation report for the period 14 July. Sorry. Are you aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can turn once again -- this one is different. On the second page, the bullet marked (D), or the section marked (D), "Southern BH command." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It says: "(1) Mostar. All UNPROFOR vehicle movement towards Mostar continues to be forbidden." This is the 14th of July. Can you comment on that and on ECMM access at this stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: That was the general situation that applied to everybody, and that also applied to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to Exhibit 3471. That's two documents further on in the binder, Exhibit 3471. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is European Community Liaison Officer Kiseljak, and it's the daily situation report, also 14 July, but this is a subsequent date. It was -- at the top we see the date 15 July. If we turn to the second page, paragraph (D) once again, and I think here we see the very same thing again. "(1) Mostar. All movements of UNPROFOR vehicles towards Mostar are forbidden." Sorry, I just wish to check that this is not the same. These are indeed two different documents. Paragraph 1: "Mostar. All the movements of UNPROFOR vehicles towards Mostar are forbidden, and also the access to Capljina." And do you have anything to add to that further to what you've already said?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: No, I can't. I don't know whether an exception had been made or whether ECMM was not able to get to Capljina either. I don't know whether it would have been possible if we had had the opportunity or the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next exhibit. That is Exhibit 3470. That's the exhibit immediately before this document we've been looking at. You have it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this is an ECMM report, a daily summary for the 15th of July, 1993, and if we look at the end, it says: "Best regards, Jesus, acting as HCC." Do you know why Jesus Amatriain would have been acting HCC at that stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: I think it was at that moment when I and Sir Martin Garrod went to a briefing to Zenica. That means that the moment that I mentioned previously, when I talked about supply vehicles in the area of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Perhaps you could repeat that name for the record.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: Yes. He was leading the HCC, Jesus Amatriain, because at that moment in time I was on the way to Zenica with Sir Martin Garrod and to get a briefing so it was a -- the plan was to go there together for the hand-over, and I mentioned this previously were supply vehicles were traveling to the lake north-west of Jablanica, or south-west of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we look at paragraph 9, the intentions and the very last sentence there: "M4 will" -- sorry not that one. The first paragraph under "Intentions." "M2 will try to enter Mostar as every day and talk to -- and talk to the soldiers and the CPs" - check-points. "Also they will try to phone the HVO authorities in Mostar in order to arrange future meetings." Can you comment on that, what's meant here?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: At that time, whoever was present had -- went daily to the western check-point, to Siroki Brijeg just not to miss any opportunity. Of course, it meant we had to use a great deal of petrol and also time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And were these successful, these efforts to enter or not? I see you were shaking your head.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: No. No, they were not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My final question on this document, and this relates back to the question of HV troops. If we look at paragraph 6, but it is indeed on the second page of the document, at the top we see: "SpaBat has provided us with the following information." And then the first bullet point: "There were heavy combats last night south of Mostar, although the city was calm." And then: "It is said that the HV troops, special forces, and the 41st HV brigade from Split are carry out a counter-attack in this area ..." Can you comment on that or did you have any other information than only that provided by SpaBat at this stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN
utterances.text: We did not have information, but I can remember that we talked about this, that Jesus Amatriain, that you heard more noises of fighting than would have been the case usually, or you might say combat noises. So that might be a confirmation of this matter, but nothing that happened right on this spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that might be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, you will give me the time used by the Prosecution. It should be around three hours. Colonel, you're under oath. Therefore, you're now the witness of the court, the witness of justice, and as such you are not allowed to have any contacts with anyone before tomorrow's hearing, and we'll resume tomorrow at 2.15. The Victims and Witnesses Unit will take care of you. Yes. I've just been told that the Prosecution has used two hours and 58 minutes. You will therefore have one hour and two minutes left, Mr. Kruger. We'll reconvene tomorrow at 2.15.
